# Combining Time Series

{{< include _setup.qmd >}}

## Problem

A daily market series and a monthly macroeconomic series cannot be joined meaningfully by exact dates. A naive inner join can discard nearly every daily observation. Forward filling the macro series can also imply that a month's value was known before publication.

## Principle

Choose the target period and aggregation rule first. Preserve the distinction between an observation date and a join key. Make join losses visible and do not impute values without a specific analytical reason.

## Example

We aggregate currency rates to the **last recorded reference observation in each completed calendar month**. “Last” does not mean “last non-missing”. HICP already has one observation per month. Both are keyed by observation month.

The last common finite month determines the endpoint. A complete 120-month grid defines the ten-year window. The default full alignment retains missing months as explicit rows, so the requested window cannot shrink silently.

```{r}
#| label: alignment-result
example$aligned$audit[c("start", "end", "requested_months", "output_rows", "join", "imputed_values")]
knitr::kable(tail(example$aligned$data[c("date", "market", "inflation", "market_observation_date",
                                       "market_observations", "inflation_source_statuses")], 6),
  col.names = c("Month", "USD per EUR", "HICP", "FX observed", "FX records", "HICP status"))
```

## Code

```r
aligned <- align_timeseries(market, inflation,
  years = 10L, market_method = "last", join = "full",
  as_of = "2026-10-11")
```

`market_method = "mean"` instead computes the arithmetic mean of all recorded observations within a month. It preserves NA if any input is missing. This is a different question from a month-end reference level. Neither calculation reconstructs a traded closing price.

```{r}
#| label: aggregation-audit
example$aligned$audit$market_aggregation
example$aligned$audit[c("market_months_outside_window", "inflation_months_outside_window",
                       "absent_market_months", "absent_inflation_months", "dropped_by_join")]
```

## Checks

The output includes `market_observation_date`, the number of daily records available in the monthly period, missing-source counts and retained provider status codes. For last-observation aggregation, only the final recorded value determines the level; the record count describes coverage. A presence flag distinguishes a genuinely absent monthly record from an existing record whose value is NA.

```{r}
#| label: alignment-contract
stopifnot(nrow(example$aligned$data) == 120L,
          anyDuplicated(example$aligned$data$date) == 0L,
          !is.unsorted(example$aligned$data$date),
          example$aligned$audit$imputed_values == 0L)
```

Inner and left joins are available as deliberate alternatives. Their dropped dates are recorded in `dropped_by_join`. This does not solve publication timing: a point-in-time analysis needs release dates and appropriate vintages before any as-of join.

## Common mistakes

- Aggregating a partial current month alongside completed months.
- Choosing the last non-missing observation and concealing a missing final value.
- Forward filling a released monthly value into days before it was available.
- Confusing weekend closure with missing business-day data.
- Reporting 120 months of history after a join has removed months without disclosure.

## Takeaway

Alignment is an analytical transformation, not a clerical join. The output should show which periods exist, which values are missing and what the transformation discarded.
